extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (persons evaluating patent subject-matter eligibility)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiners on applying 35 U.S.C. §101/Alice–Mayo eligibility framework including when to use a streamlined analysis, how to formulate and support rejections, and evidentiary requirements. Covers identification of judicial exceptions, evaluation of additional elements, and examples of limitations that do not impart eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-of-use / technological-environment limitations do not make an abstract idea eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that merely limit an abstract idea to a particular technological environment or field of use (e.g., use on the Internet, in a telephone network, in a power-grid context, in a telephone network or Internet, in petrochemical industries, or on a generic computer) generally do not provide meaningful limits on the claim and therefore do not render the claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides multiple examples and cited cases (FairWarning v. Iatric Sys.; Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec; Electric Power Group v. Alstom; Genetic Techs. v. Merial; Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One; Ultramercial v. Hulu; buySAFE v. Google; Parker v. Flook). Examiners should consider the terms “technological environment” and “field of use” interchangeably and recognize overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity (see MPEP §2106.05(g)). If a limitation generally links use of a judicial exception to a technological environment, the examiner should explain why that limitation does not meaningfully limit the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) when eligibility is self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may use a streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) for efficiency when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (e.g., the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality), concluding eligibility without a full Alice/Mayo analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The result of the streamlined analysis will always be the same as the full analysis; it is not a way to avoid a finding of ineligibility. If doubt exists about whether the applicant is seeking coverage for a judicial exception, the full analysis should be used. The record may simply reflect eligibility by the absence of a §101 rejection or include clarifying remarks. Examples include claims to clear technological improvements (robotic arm control system, artificial hip prosthesis with a naturally occurring mineral coating). See MPEP §2106.05(a) and cited cases (Enfish; McRO). Use Pathway A only when eligibility is self-evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility is self-evident — when to avoid full analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that may recite a judicial exception but, when viewed as a whole, clearly does not attempt to tie up the exception (and clearly does not prevent others from practicing the exception) may be eligible without the full analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: complex manufactured industrial products or processes with meaningful limitations; claims that merely include ancillary nature-based components (e.g., cellphone with a gold electrical contact). If a claim is a 'close call' on whether it improves technology or computer functionality, perform the full analysis (BASCOM example). Streamlined analysis appropriate only when self-evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear improvement to technology or computer functionality avoids abstract-idea characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to clear improvements in computer-related technology or computer functionality are not necessarily abstract and therefore may avoid the full eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites cases such as Enfish (self-referential table) and McRO (automatic lip synchronization) where claims were found eligible at Step 1. An examiner could reasonably find such claims eligible at Pathway A or B. See MPEP §2106.05(a) for details on what constitutes an improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections must be based on substantive law and supported to establish a prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility rejections must be grounded in substantive law under 35 U.S.C. §101 as interpreted by judicial precedent; examination guidance/examples do not themselves form a legal basis for rejection. Examiners must review the entire record and make claim-by-claim determinations. When a claim is likely ineligible, the examiner must formulate an Office action that sets forth a prima facie case of ineligibility that is clear and specific enough to give applicant sufficient notice to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should review specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law, and prior art. Dependent claims must be considered separately (they can be eligible even if an independent claim is not, and vice versa). If rejection is maintained after applicant response, examiner must provide rebuttal. See MPEP §2106.03–.07 for procedural details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim (Step 2A Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: A §101 rejection must point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recite or describe the judicial exception and explain why those limitations are considered an exception (e.g., fall within abstract idea groupings or are a law of nature/product of nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For abstract ideas, the examiner should identify how the claim limitation maps to the abstract idea groupings (mathematical concepts, mental processes, certain methods of organizing human activity) or, if outside those groupings, follow the 'tentative abstract idea' procedure and justify treatment as an abstract idea (may cite precedent). For laws of nature or natural phenomena, identify and provide a reasoned rationale. For products of nature, explain why the claimed product lacks markedly different characteristics from its natural counterpart. Sample explanatory language is provided in the MPEP (e.g., comparing collected information to a threshold = mental process). Examiners should be familiar with cited decisions and avoid relying on non-precedential decisions unless facts match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and evaluate additional claim elements for integration into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying the judicial exception, the rejection should identify any additional claim elements beyond the exception and evaluate whether those elements, individually and in combination, integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the considerations in MPEP §§2106.04(d), 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). Give weight to all claimed additional elements, even if they are well-understood, routine, conventional. Explain why the additional elements do not integrate the exception into a practical application (or explain why they do). Address combinations of elements because a new combination of known steps may be patent eligible (Diamond v. Diehr). Provide clear rationale so applicant can respond effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why additional elements do not amount to 'significantly more' (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: When concluding that claim is directed to a judicial exception and does not provide an inventive concept, the rejection must explain why the additional elements, taken individually and as a combination, do not result in the claim as a whole amounting to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If particular claim limitations are found to be well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the rejection must explicitly support that factual conclusion in writing (see evidentiary requirements below). For generic computer elements performing generic functions (e.g., using the Internet to gather data), explain why such generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim; consider DDR Holdings and MPEP §2106.05(f) for examples where combinations of generic components were nevertheless not merely generic. See MPEP §2106.05 for additional considerations (insignificant extra-solution activity, field-of-use limitations, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary support required when asserting elements are well-understood, routine, conventional (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner should not assert that additional claim elements (or combinations) are well-understood, routine, or conventional unless the examiner expressly supports the rejection in writing with one or more specified forms of evidence or authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three permissible supports: (A) citation to an express statement in the specification or to a statement by applicant during prosecution demonstrating that the element is well-understood/routine/conventional (e.g., described as commercially available or so well-known that particulars are not described); (B) citation to one or more court decisions discussed in MPEP §2106.05(d) that note the well-understood/routine/conventional nature of the element(s) (ensure the claim limitations match the court-found elements at the same level of generality); (C) citation to a publication demonstrating the element is well-understood/routine/conventional (book, manual, review article, etc.). A finding cannot be based solely on specification silence. See examples and cautions in MPEP §2106.05(d) and related subsections.

rubrics_metrics.name: No general requirement for evidence when identifying the judicial exception (Step 2A Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because courts treat identification of judicial exceptions largely as a question of law, examiners are not required to rely on extrinsic evidence (publications, affidavits) to find that a claim recites a judicial exception at Step 2A Prong One.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites cases (FairWarning; OIP Techs.; Content Extraction). However, the issue of whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional may be a factual issue, and in those instances factual support is required (see Berkheimer, Interval Licensing, Rapid Litig.). Thus: no evidence required to identify an exception, but evidence/support required if asserting well-understood/routine/conventional in Step 2B (see above).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components/functions at high level of generality do not necessarily confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that recite generic computer components performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality (e.g., using the Internet to gather data) typically do not meaningfully limit an abstract idea and thus often do not render a claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should explain why such generic computing functions fail to add meaningful limitations. Keep in mind DDR Holdings where courts found that certain computer-implemented combinations were significantly more than abstract ideas; consider whether claimed generic components, in combination, perform functions that are not merely generic. See MPEP §2106.05(f) for court-found examples of mere instructions to implement an exception on a computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity and overlap with field-of-use limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Data-gathering steps limited to particular data sources or types (e.g., Internet, power grid data, XML tags) may be both insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use limitations; such limitations often do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and case citations (Ultramercial; Electric Power; Intellectual Ventures v. Erie Indem.). Examiners should carefully consider each claim on its merits and evaluate overlapping considerations; explain in the rejection why such extra-solution or field-of-use limitations are insignificant or fail to provide meaningful limitation. See MPEP §2106.05(g) and (h).

rubrics_metrics.name: When making a rejection, explain each part of the Step 2 analysis in the Office action
rubrics_metrics.description: A Step 2 rejection should separately explain Step 2A Prong One (identify and justify the judicial exception), Step 2A Prong Two (identify additional elements and evaluate integration into a practical application) and Step 2B (explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP provides procedural bullets: For Prong One identify the exception and why; for Prong Two identify additional elements and evaluate integration using MPEP considerations; for Step 2B explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more, and if asserting routine/conventional, provide one of the evidentiary supports. The rejection must provide sufficient clarity and specificity to enable applicant to effectively respond. See sample explanations in the MPEP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution and stating all non-cumulative rejections in the first Office action
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of a §101 rejection, examiners must perform complete examination for every claim under other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, 101 utility/inventorship/double patenting and non-statutory double patenting) and state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural obligation to ensure compact prosecution; do not withhold other rejections when issuing a §101 rejection. Provide all non-cumulative grounds to allow applicant to respond comprehensively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practice: consult specification for amendable elements to overcome a §101 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a rejection, it is a best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine whether there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible, and if so, identify and suggest them in the Office action as ways to overcome the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides constructive guidance to applicants and helps clarify the record. Suggesting claim amendments that would result in eligibility is encouraged when appropriate.
